dashboard.label: Feed administration
dashboard.description: Upload and import offline vulnerability databases. This app never reaches the network itself.

div.p: This app makes no outbound network requests, by design: it is built to run on a search head with no route to the internet. Vulnerability data gets in exactly one way — you build a bundle on a machine that does have access, carry it across, and import it here.
div.h4: 1. Build a bundle (on a connected machine)
div.pre:
riskability-feed sources # what can be fetched
riskability-feed build --out riskability-feed.tar.gz \ --ecosystem Ubuntu --ecosystem Debian --ecosystem Alpine \ --ecosystem npm --ecosystem PyPI --ecosystem Go --ecosystem Maven \ --kev --epss
div.p: Only the sources you name are downloaded. Pick the distributions and language ecosystems your fleet actually runs; the Coverage dashboard shows which component types are going unmatched, which is the fastest way to work out what to add next.
div.h4: 2. Get it onto this search head
div.p: Either drop the file straight into the staging directory shown above — the right choice for anything large, since nothing has to fit in memory — or use the upload control, which is capped at 64 MB because a REST upload is held whole in the search head's memory.
Import replaces the active feed rather than merging into it, so withdrawn advisories and corrected ranges cannot survive as ghosts. Searches keep seeing the previous feed until the import finishes.
div.h4: Windows estates need one extra source
div.p: Linux packages are installed by a package manager, so each carries a PURL and can be matched against its distribution's own advisories — which is what makes backport handling possible. Windows software has no equivalent: there is no package manager and no PURL, only a display name and a version read out of the registry.
So a Windows fleet needs NVD in the bundle, which carries CPE-keyed ranges:
div.pre: riskability-feed build --out riskability-feed.tar.gz \ --nvd 2015-2026 --mitre --kev --epss \ --ecosystem Ubuntu --ecosystem npm # keep your Linux sources too
div.p: Two things to expect. Every Windows finding is reported at low confidence, because the component is tied to an advisory through a CPE generated from a display name (“7-Zip 24.08 (x64)” → cpe:2.3:a:igor_pavlov:7-zip:24.08) rather than read from a package record. The version comparison may be exact while the product identity is still a guess, so these are leads to verify, not facts to report. And installed hotfixes are collected but not yet matched: assessing Windows OS patches properly means asking “is the KB that fixes this CVE installed” against Microsoft’s MSRC data, which is a different mechanism from version ranges and is not implemented yet.
div.h4: If this search head does have internet access
div.p: Use the Fetch directly panel above. It checks which upstream hosts are actually reachable first, so an air-gapped instance tells you immediately rather than starting a download that fails minutes later. The app makes no outbound request unless you press that button — nothing is scheduled and nothing runs at install time.

The feeds carry different licences: OSV aggregates sources that are individually CC‑BY‑4.0 (GitHub, Red Hat), CC‑BY‑SA‑4.0 (Ubuntu), MIT (AlmaLinux) and BSD (Rocky); CISA KEV is US‑government public domain; EPSS is published by FIRST and expects attribution. Each record keeps the source it came from, so attribution survives into Splunk. Building a bundle for your own organisation is uncontroversial; redistributing one is a decision for you rather than for this app, which is exactly why nothing is shipped pre-loaded.
